definitions.definition: A theory describing gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy.
definitions.example: Like a heavy ball on a rubber sheet making a dent that pulls other objects toward it.

definitions.definition: A theory describing the behavior of very small particles, where outcomes are only probable, not certain.
definitions.example: Like a spinning coin that is both heads and tails until you look at it.

definitions.definition: The underlying layer or foundation of reality that everything else is built on.
definitions.example: Like the canvas of a painting that holds all the paint.

definitions.definition: A break or split in something that was once whole.
definitions.example: Like a crack in a window that separates it into two pieces.

definitions.definition: The state of two things not being able to work together or be true at the same time.
definitions.example: Like trying to fit a square peg into a round hole.

definitions.definition: Describing a system where every event is caused by previous events, with no randomness.
definitions.example: Like a row of dominoes falling one after another in a fixed order.

definitions.definition: Describing a system where outcomes are based on chance, not certainty.
definitions.example: Like rolling a die and only knowing the chance of each number, not which one will come up.

definitions.definition: The idea that the act of observing or measuring something can change its behavior.
definitions.example: Like checking if a light is on by opening the door, which lets in light and changes the room.

definitions.definition: A mathematical description of all possible states a quantum particle can be in.
definitions.example: Like a blurry photo that shows all possible positions of a moving ball at once.

definitions.definition: An extremely tiny length (about 1.6 x 10^-35 meters) where the effects of gravity and quantum mechanics become equally important.
definitions.example: Like a ruler so small that it's a trillion trillion times smaller than a grain of sand.

definitions.definition: The attempt to combine two different theories into one single, consistent theory.
definitions.example: Like trying to merge two different maps of the same city into one accurate map.

definitions.definition: A theory that suggests particles are tiny vibrating strings, but it has many possible versions and no experimental proof.
definitions.example: Like a musical instrument that can play many tunes, but you can't test which tune is real.

definitions.definition: A theory that says spacetime is made of tiny loops or chunks, not smooth.
definitions.example: Like a digital photo made of pixels instead of a smooth painting.

definitions.definition: In Christian theology, the event where Adam and Eve disobeyed God, bringing sin and brokenness into the world.
definitions.example: Like a perfect machine that gets a crack and starts malfunctioning.

definitions.definition: Referring to a change that affects the fundamental layer of reality, not just surface details.
definitions.example: Like changing the foundation of a house, not just the paint color.

definitions.definition: Connected or linked so that changes in one affect the other.
definitions.example: Like two gears that turn together when one moves.

definitions.definition: In physics, describing a system where all parts are in sync and act as one unified whole.
definitions.example: Like a choir singing the same note in perfect harmony.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'Word' or 'Reason,' used in the Bible to describe Jesus as the divine principle that holds everything together.
definitions.example: Like the operating system that keeps a computer running smoothly.

definitions.definition: A proposed field that represents the coherence or unity of reality, often linked to the Logos.
definitions.example: Like an invisible force field that keeps everything connected and orderly.

definitions.definition: A mathematical rule that describes when a system is fully unified and without breaks.
definitions.example: Like a rule that says all parts of a puzzle must fit perfectly without gaps.

definitions.definition: A mathematical equation saying that the chi-field has no sources or sinks, meaning it is perfectly balanced and coherent.
definitions.example: Like a river with no leaks or extra water added, flowing smoothly.

definitions.definition: A way of matching two different things so that their structures are exactly the same, even if the details differ.
definitions.example: Like a map of a subway system that matches the real tracks, even if the map is smaller.

definitions.definition: The idea that a system retains information about its original, unbroken state.
definitions.example: Like a broken vase that still shows the shape of the original vase in its pieces.

definitions.definition: Describing a system that has lost its internal synchronization and behaves randomly or independently.
definitions.example: Like a crowd of people all talking at once instead of chanting together.

definitions.definition: Describing something that comes in discrete, separate packets rather than a continuous flow.
definitions.example: Like stairs instead of a ramp, where you can only be on one step at a time.

definitions.definition: Describing an effect that seems to influence the past, not just the future.
definitions.example: Like sending a message back in time to change what happened earlier.

definitions.definition: Describing a connection between two things that are far apart, without any physical link between them.
definitions.example: Like two dancers who move in sync even if they are in different rooms.

definitions.definition: A level of similarity where two things match in some ways but not in structure.
definitions.example: Like a photo and a painting of the same person—they look similar but are not identical.

definitions.definition: A strong match where two things have the same structure, so you can map one onto the other perfectly.
definitions.example: Like two different puzzles that have the same shape of pieces, just different pictures.

definitions.definition: The condition that the important relationships within a system stay the same when you map it to another system.
definitions.example: Like a family tree that keeps the same parent-child connections even if you redraw it.

definitions.definition: The property that a mapping is forced and not just a random choice.
definitions.example: Like a key that only fits one lock, not any lock you pick.

definitions.definition: A rule or limit that restricts what is possible.
definitions.example: Like a speed limit that tells you how fast you can drive.

definitions.definition: The property that a mapping works both ways, so each side gives information about the other.
definitions.example: Like a two-way mirror where you can see both sides.

definitions.definition: A perfect one-to-one matching where every element in one set is paired with exactly one in the other, and vice versa.
definitions.example: Like assigning each student a unique locker number, with no lockers left empty.

definitions.definition: Specific conditions that, if met, would prove a theory wrong.
definitions.example: Like a test that says 'if this happens, my idea is false.'

definitions.definition: Information gained through observation or experiment, not just theory.
definitions.example: Like measuring the temperature outside instead of guessing.

definitions.definition: A mathematical proof showing that quantum mechanics cannot be explained by hidden variables and must involve non-local connections.
definitions.example: Like proving that two coins flipped far apart can still be mysteriously linked.

definitions.definition: A statistical measure of how unlikely a result is due to chance; 6σ means a result is extremely significant (about 1 in a billion chance of being random).
definitions.example: Like a test score so high that it's almost impossible to get by luck.

definitions.definition: The idea that human consciousness can interact with or influence physical systems, especially in quantum experiments.
definitions.example: Like thinking about a coin and making it land on heads more often.

definitions.definition: An experimental outcome where no effect is found, meaning the hypothesis is not supported.
definitions.example: Like testing if a new medicine works and finding no difference from a sugar pill.

definitions.definition: A gradual change from one state to another, like a slope.
definitions.example: Like a color fading from dark blue to light blue.

definitions.definition: Describing things large enough to be seen with the naked eye, not microscopic.
definitions.example: Like a car or a tree, not an atom.
